items.content:
01
Introduction
Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available
here
and
here
.
Introduction
Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.
One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called
holographic duality
. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.
The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.
The first problem
Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.
In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists
set out the calculation that would settle the question
, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It showed that the phase transition
is
abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.
The second problem
concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called
bootstrapping
.
Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.
Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.
Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.
In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.
A note about Claude’s methods
In August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.
The agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.
The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result
recently proved by an OpenAI model
. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.
The Hawking-Page transition
To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through New York City.
Two equally good routes from Penn Station (A) to the High Line entrance (B). In theory, a quantum particle can take both simultaneously.
Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.
This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.
The double-slit experiment. When electrons are fired one at a time from a source (A) toward a barrier with two slits, each lands at a single point on the screen. The hits build up a pattern of stripes that is only possible if each one passed through both slits.
To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its
possible histories
. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.
This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.
Hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.
Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the
cosmological constant
, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.
At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.
Which history wins depends on temperature. Below the Hawking-Page temperature (black line), the universe is filled with a gas of particles, including gravitons; above it, the universe contains a black hole.
It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.
This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.
In the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.
In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it
to a new level of precision
.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?
For now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as
weak coupling
. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.
Remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, showed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.
When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps
loops
. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.
The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual issue, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.
To solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.
The result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.
This is a beautiful outcome. It shows that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.
Many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please
don’t
do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.)
Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.
Another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.
The modular bootstrap
As we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.
As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10
-35
meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.
Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.
Remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the
3D critical Ising model
, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.
In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the
modular bootstrap
, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.
Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.
To understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.
Three possible shapes of spacetime in 3D gravity: a ball, a donut (or torus), and a two-holed donut. The spacetime is the inside of each shape, and the quantum theory is “written” on its surface.
The modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or
torus
. There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.
Two ways to interpret the same donut-shaped spacetime. (left) Time runs the long way around the hole, and space is represented by the shorter loop; (right) space runs the long way around, and time is represented by the shorter loop.
In calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.
Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.
Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter
which
loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.
If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.
The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?
This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.
The goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.
Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The
results
of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a
ceiling
of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.
Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a
spectral curve
. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.
This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.
Conclusion
These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.

items.text: bhis-blog published: Threat Hunting On The Network: An Active Search for Risks on the Wire
items.title: Threat Hunting On The Network: An Active Search for Risks on the Wire
items.content:
All threat hunters are looking for evidence of nefarious activity, hopefully before an incident happens. Threat hunting on the network involves actively searching through packet data for malicious activity. Threat hunting on an endpoint depends more heavily on logs. Think of it as on the wire (or in the air) versus on a host itself. Don’t worry, you don’t have to look through every packet in a pcap file. That would make your head explode!
We would like to think our firewalls and Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems (IDS or IPS) are blocking all evil traffic from coming in, but those appliances have limits. Adversaries evolve their techniques faster than the static signatures used on our perimeter defenses. Updates from vendors and threat intelligence feeds can’t keep up. A network threat hunter looks for patterns beyond specific byte sequences, file hashes, and documented signature exploits.
In contrast to signatures, behavior analysis lets network threat hunters draw insights from network baselines to understand expected protocols and traffic flows. Threat actors may change their techniques and procedures, but they still have fundamental network behaviors.
Signature-Based vs Behavioral Analysis in Threat Hunting
Common Data Sources
NetFlow or Internet Protocol Flow Information Export (IPFIX) records
Every switch, router, firewall, VPN appliance, IDS/IPS, or other network device capable of exporting flow data should be sending these flow records to the SIEM.
HTTP/HTTPs Proxy logs for TLS/HTTP headers
VPN appliance logs for external connections to internal resources
Full packet captures
Pcap files captured from taps or SPAN sessions.
My Favorite Tools
NetFlow/IPFIX/logs > SIEM (Wazuh or Graylog) for aggregation and metadata
Logs and/or packets > Elasticsearch > Kibana for log analysis and visualization
Packets > Zeek > RITA by Active Countermeasures for full packet capture, indexing, alerting, and search
Packets > Arkime for full packet capture, indexing, and search
Packets > Wireshark or TShark for deep analysis
A Few Additional Indicators
Unusual port usage:
services running on non-standard ports.
DNS anomalies:
DGA domains, DNS tunneling, or excessive NXDOMAIN responses.
Failed authentication attempts:
brute force indicators across multiple systems.
Certificate anomalies:
mismatched common names or short validity periods.
TLS/SSL anomalies:
weak ciphers, unusual JA3/JA4+ hashes, or certificate chain issues.
My Favorite Methodologies
Crown jewel analysis
— Focus on protecting most critical assets and data.
Hypothesis-driven hunting
— Form theories about potential threats and test them.
Kill chain mapping
— Identify which attack phase the indicators belong to.
Assumed breach methodology
— Operate as though compromise has already occurred.
Take advantage of established frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK®, Pyramid of Pain, PEAK.
A good network threat hunter is also looking at internal traffic. Is Susie in Accounting supposed to be using SSH to access a server in another country? No. What about Brad in Marketing? Is it normal for him to download multi-gigabyte files from a server in the data center? Maybe. At three o’clock in the morning? Probably not.
Finally, don’t be afraid to dive in. Threat hunting is not just for the most experienced cybersecurity analysts. Start with a single protocol and tools you already have to build confidence.

For more information about these vulnerabilities, see the Details section of this advisory. For additional information on these vulnerabilities in ClamAV, see the ClamAV blog . Cisco has released software updates that address these vulnerabilities in affected Cisco platforms. There are no workarounds that address these vulnerabilities. Notes: The Security Impact Rating (SIR) for these vulnerabilities is High only for Windows-based platforms because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a privileged security context. The platforms that are highly impacted include Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector for Windows. The SIR for these vulnerabilities is Medium on other platforms, including Linux and Mac platforms, because those platforms run the ClamAV scanning process in a lower-privileged security context. The affected platforms include Secure Endpoint Connector for Linux and Mac. Cisco Secure Endpoint Private Cloud itself is not impacted by these vulnerabilities. Instead, the Cisco Secure Endpoint Connector software is impacted. items.title: 报告称 DeepSeek-V4-Flash 用上 NVIDIA 禁运显卡：AI 硬件侧信道的三种路径
items.content:
11 月中旬，
Unemployment
Labs 发布报告
，指出他们仅凭公开下载的模型权重，就推断出
DeepSeek-V4-Flash、Kimi K3
等六款中国新模型在初始化阶段用到了受美国出口管制限制的 NVIDIA Blackwell
显卡。由于这一代芯片属于对华禁运硬件，这份报告很快在业内引发关注。
撇开合规争议，这项研究真正有意思的是背后的取证逻辑：模型训练完、权重文件公开发布之后，里面怎么还会留着显卡型号的痕迹？把视角再放大一点，从最初生成权重、低精度训练到最后上线提供推理服务，硬件的物理特性在每一步都有机会透进数据或输出里。下面先讲清楚这份报告是怎么从权重里读出显卡型号的，再顺着模型生命周期看看另外两条侧信道，以及它们眼下的实际成色和防堵成本。
训练结束后，权重里为什么还留着初始显卡的痕迹？
训练开始前，PyTorch
会把整张权重矩阵当成一条有几亿个格子的长带子，调用 NVIDIA 的 Philox
算法往里面填满随机初始值。为了填得快，显卡上的所有并行计算单元 SM
会一起开工，每个 SM 固定派出一支两千多人的施工小队。不同显卡的 SM
数量不同：H100 有 132 个 SM，全场一共约 27 万名工人同时上阵；B200 有 148
个 SM，GB200 有 152 个 SM，全场总人数分别增加到约 30 万和 31 万。
给定同一颗随机种子，每条线程自己生成的数字序列完全固定：无论在哪张卡上，同一编号的线程算出的第
1 个数、第 2
个数都一模一样。但往权重矩阵里填数时，全场所有线程是按编号轮流一格一格往下填的。看下面这张
3 行 4 列的简化示意图就明白了：左边的小显卡假设只有 A、B、C
三条线程轮流填，前 3 格填完第一轮，第 4 格就立刻轮到线程 A
填第二轮的数，一路顺延下来，最底下那一行填进去了
C3, A4, B4, C4
。右边换一张大显卡，多了一条线程
D，变成四条线程轮流填，正好每行 4
格填满一轮，最底下那一行填进去的就变成了
A3, B3, C3, D3
。
明明随机种子一模一样，每条线程各自生成的数字也没变，可仅仅因为参与轮流填表的线程总数变了，每一轮的跨度不同，越往后的行错位就越远。在真实模型里，面对第几亿个格子，H100
和 B200 填进同一行里的，早就变成了完全不同线程在不同轮次生成的数字。
同一随机种子在 H100 与 B200
上写入权重矩阵的坐标差异
那为什么最底下那一行能保留到训练结束？这跟词表矩阵的更新方式有关。神经网络中间层的参数是每读一句话就全员一起更新，唯独开头的词表矩阵是按词对号入座的：训练语料里实际出现了哪个词，才只更新那个词对应的那一行；只要某个词从头到尾没出现过，它那一行参数就纹丝不动。而在真实大模型里，总有一批行一次都不会出现：既有预训练语料里没撞上的极冷门符号、或是专门留给后续对话微调的预留标记，也有工程师为了让矩阵行数凑够
128
的整数倍、在词表末尾顺手补出来的几百个凑整空行。这些行里的数字从头到尾没有更新过，原封不动保留着初始化时的状态，而且它们排在词表第几行、对应第几个格子，打开公开下载的权重文件直接就能看到。
既然知道末尾未训练行的确切位置，外部研究者就不用去反推打乱的顺序，直接正着重算一遍去对答案就行：先假定一颗随机种子，再分别按
H100 和 B200
的线程总数与轮流规则，直接算出末尾未训练行那个位置该填哪些数，拿去跟下载的权重文件比对。因为
PyTorch 默认的随机种子总共只有约 43
亿种可能，研究团队直接用穷举法把全部种子和常见显卡线程数试了一遍，累计核查约
6
万亿种组合。只要种子或显卡型号猜错，算出来的数就跟文件里的未训练行毫无关系；一旦两者同时猜中，整行几千个数字就会逐位对上，相关系数超过
0.999。
靠这套办法，他们在 DeepSeek-V4-Flash、Kimi K3 和 MiniMax-M3
等六款中国新模型里匹配出 Blackwell 排布，而更早的 DeepSeek-V3 和同期的
GLM-5 等则对应上一代 Hopper。为了验证结果，团队真机租用了 H100 和
GB200，现场重算出与 DeepSeek-V3 及 Kimi K3
完全一致的未用行。他们还专门比对了 AMD MI300X 显卡的计算单元排布，确认
DeepSeek-V4-Flash 的特征只指向 NVIDIA，随后把
复现代码
全部开源。
一天后，开发者 Bojie Li 发布了
独立复现报告
与
扩展扫描工具
。他在两百多个开源模型里找出了
185 个硬件线程指纹，除了中国模型，也涵盖 NVIDIA Nemotron
等海外型号。
那如果词表里没留原封不动的空位，是不是就查不出来了？未必。在小米
MiMo-V2.5-Pro-Base
里，词表每一行都参与了训练，最终权重等于初始随机数加上训练改变量。因为训练改变量远大于初始值，单拿任何一行去和初始序列比对，相似度都微乎其微；可一旦把上万行数据放在一起同时比对，不同词的训练改变量方向各异、在统计上互相抵消，唯独真正的初始序列能在每一行里都贡献一点正向吻合，累积起来就能把
Hopper
排布清晰地凸现出来。还有一种常见情况是训练开启了权重衰减：算法每走一步，都会给所有参数乘上一个略小于一的正数，让数值整体往零缩小。在
Qwen2-7B
里，那些没参与训练的空位行一路缩到了存储格式能表示的最小非零值，所有数字的绝对值全都变得一样；但因为每次只是乘以正数，正负号从来没有翻转过，光靠核对整行加减号的排列顺序，依然能把
Hopper 的初始序列锁定出来。
当然，这套方法也有明确的技术边界。它只能看清生成初始权重那一刻用了什么规格的显卡，而且只要两款显卡的
SM
数量相同，全场总人数就一样，单靠排布无法进一步区分。至于初始化完成之后，漫长的正式训练有没有一直留在同款显卡上，静态权重本身给不出直接证明，因为中途随时可以把权重存盘、挪到别的集群继续训练。
改用 CPU
初始化就会失效，静态权重里还有别的线索吗？
初始化指纹虽然查得准，但厂商想要抹掉它并不难。在 Bojie Li
扫描的模型里，就有几十个模型读不出这套指纹：有的直接用 CPU
单线程顺序生成初始权重，有的在训练结束后用 CPU
随机数覆盖了词表末尾的空位，还有像 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
这样虽然留着看似未动的空位行，却对不上已知显卡排布和随机种子，多半是更换了初始化代码。只要避开显卡默认的并行初始化流程，前一条线索就会彻底断掉。
如果初始化改到了 CPU
上，训练出来的权重里还会留下显卡自己的算术痕迹吗？理论上还有一条线索，来自低精度训练的分组缩放方式。为了省显存、提速度，现在训练大模型常把高精度参数压缩成
8 比特甚至 4 比特的低精度格式。4
比特除去正负号，本身只能表示零点五、一、一点五、二、三、四、六等寥寥几个固定刻度；要想拿它装下大小悬殊的真实权重，工程上必须把相邻的权重分成小队，给每个小队配一个共同的缩放倍率，让队里所有数字都表示成这个倍率乘以上述固定刻度。根据
NVIDIA
的技术介绍
，上一代 Hopper 主推的 8
比特格式，通常按上百个参数甚至整张矩阵共用一个倍率；而新一代 Blackwell
原生支持的 4 比特格式，硬件规定每 16 个相邻参数就得单独配一个倍率。
这种硬件格式差异为什么可能留痕？因为在同一个小队内部，所有数字都是同一个倍率乘以那几个固定刻度算出来的，彼此之间的比值落在同一套网格上；一旦跨进下一小队，倍率就会重新换一套。理论上，检测权重矩阵里是不是每
16 个元素就出现一次倍率切换，就能分辨出底层是不是跑在 Blackwell
的原生低精度硬件流水线上。不过这条路眼下还停留在原理推演阶段：模型预训练完通常还要经历高精度微调与强化学习，发布前也会转回常规格式重新打包，后续的连续数值改动会把原本整齐的网格冲淡，目前社区也还没有做出能跨大批量模型稳定提取这种信号的开源工具。
只开在线 API
时，还能试探出推理机房的显卡吗？
前面两条路都得先拿到公开的权重文件，查的是模型出厂前用过什么卡。如果模型已经上线，只对外提供一个黑盒聊天接口，既不透露机房里插了什么卡，也不公开后台跑的推理软件和量化精度，外部还能试探出底细吗？这要看接口背后跑的模型本身有没有开源权重，测试思路分成两路。
第一路是云厂商托管开源模型这类已知权重的情况。就算拿不到后台权限，大模型的吐字结果本身也会暴露底层硬件的算术差异。计算机做浮点数加法时，先加前两个数还是先加后两个数，末尾最后一位会出现细微的舍入差异；
Thinking
Machines Lab
的技术分析
就曾演示过，哪怕把采样温度设为零、彻底关掉随机抽签，仅仅因为服务端并行求和的先后顺序微调，算出来的候选词得分就会在小数点后好几位发生轻微漂移。
不同代际的显卡和不同的推理软件，在切分矩阵乘法和并行汇总求和时，采用的归约顺序各有固定套路。平时小数点后几位的差别不会影响哪个词排第一；可一旦碰上两个候选词得分咬得极紧，最后一位的舍入差异就足以让冠亚军互换，改写模型吐出的下一个字，并在后续生成里一路放大。NeurIPS
论文
《大语言模型推理系统指纹识别》
正是利用这一点：测试者先用本地的开源权重筛选出一批特殊提问，故意制造两个候选词得分几乎打平的临界场面，再把这些提问发给线上接口，看它每次偏向哪个词，就能反推出后台的软硬件组合。在论文的测试基准里，把采样温度设为零时，这套提问探针识别底层显卡型号、推理引擎和注意力计算后端的准确率达到了百分之百；就算把温度调到
0.3
引入随机采样，多测几次后识别显卡型号与推理引擎的平均准确率依然接近八成。由于想堵住这条路就得把不同芯片和软件栈的底层浮点运算对齐到一字不差，工程上防起来相当棘手。
第二路则是连权重都不公开的纯闭源接口。没法在本地预筛临界提问，外部就只能从吐字速度上摸硬件的物理天花板。大模型逐字生成回答时，每蹦出一个新字，都得把参与计算的模型权重从显存搬进计算单元重读一遍，所以吐字快慢直接受限于显存每秒能搬运多少数据。以机房主力的高带宽
SXM 规格为例，上一代 H100 的显存带宽是 3.35 TB/s，新一代 B200 则跃升到了
8.0
TB/s，达到前者的两倍多；与此同时，如果后台把权重精度压缩一半，每生成一个字需要搬运的数据量减半，吐字速度同样会大幅加快。
这也决定了单纯测速的局限性：面对既不公布参数规模、也不透露压缩方案的闭源服务，外部单看吐字变快，没法直接断定是机房换上了带宽翻倍的新显卡，还是工程师把模型压得更轻了。黑盒测速真正量出来的，其实是显存带宽上限与权重压缩程度共同划出的一道性能边界。
三条路径的信号强度与绕过代价
模型生命周期三条硬件侧信道在实证力度与防御代价上的对比
顺着模型从出厂到上线的全流程盘点下来，这三条路径的证据强度和防堵成本恰好形成鲜明反差。Philox
初始化排布已经在 185
个开源模型上验出了确凿指纹，是目前实证最扎实的一条路；但它的防堵成本也最低，厂商只要改用
CPU 初始化，或者在训练结束后把词表空位覆盖掉，这条线索就会立刻失效。
低精度训练的分组缩放痕迹绑在显卡原生的算术格式上，哪怕换用 CPU
初始化也绕不开。不过它目前还停留在机制推演阶段，后续的高精度微调与格式转换都会冲淡这种周期性网格，社区里也还没有出现经过大规模跨模型验证的检测工具。
真正能直接试探线上黑盒服务的，是推理阶段的算术分歧与速度边界。对于托管开源权重的接口，利用临界提问放大底层浮点加法差异，已经在实验里拿下了很高的软硬件识别率，而且极难在工程上彻底抹平；对于完全闭源的接口，吐字测速虽然点不出具体显卡的名字，却依然能摸到显存带宽与量化压缩共同决定的物理上限。软件工程向来擅长用抽象层把底层硬件藏在幕后，但在大模型密集并行与低精度算术的放大镜下，机房里的芯片依然会在权重矩阵和接口响应里留下自己的印记。

items.text: yage-share published: 不用额外埋点，如何用手头的本地日志给 AI 工具做降智尸检
items.title: 不用额外埋点，如何用手头的本地日志给 AI 工具做降智尸检
items.content:
每天高强度使用 Claude Code、Cursor 或 OpenCode
等工具的码农可能都有过这样的体验：前一天还在享受能够进行跨文件重构的智能编程助手的快感，第二天早上就发现
AI
开始说胡话，不仅无视项目的要求，甚至完全不看目标文件就大段修改。这时候去看官方的状态页面一片全绿，网上最新的模型跑分榜也是风平浪静。这到底是谁的问题？是厂商偷偷降低了配置？还是我改坏了本地的提示词和配置？
为什么公开的跑分榜看不到这种日常退化，其实是有明确的机制原因的。从
2026 年 10 月下旬开始，很多 Claude Opus 5.5 的重度用户开始抱怨 Opus 5.5
经常无视指令。但是如果你访问
LiveNerf
的每日评测项目
的话，可以看到这个连续测了 50
多天的公开监测站依然显示各项得分平稳如初。这主要是因为它受制于订阅配额，每天最多只能测
78 道题目。作者上线前实测发现，即使后台真的直接把 Opus 5.5
换成了上一代旧模型 Opus
5，这套题测出来的分数差距也在正常误差范围内，并不会触发警报。要想看到 2
个百分点的准确率波动，每周需要消耗将近一半的订阅额度。此外，它为了控制变量，特意在没有任何文件且禁用一切工具的空目录里考单轮做题，自然测不出多轮工具调用里的失常。
幸运的是，我们并不需要为此自购题库或预先部署监控插件。只要你的编程工具在本地硬盘中自动留存了
.jsonl
格式的本地会话日志，例如保存在
~/.claude/projects/
目录中的历史文本记录，里面就已经完整记录了每一轮对话的提问、模型回答、工具调用和账单明细。今年春天
AMD AI 总监 Stella Laurenzo 发布的
4
月本地日志审计报告
，以及近期一位重度订阅用户撰写的
10
月本地日志审计报告
，相继演示了一种零成本的取证思路。我们直接盘点手头现成的历史记录，就能把模糊的体感变成精确到小时的证据，还能指导手头的日常开发如何避坑。
怎么证明不是我改坏了自己的配置？
怀疑模型突然变差了，首先应该排查的是不是自己这边变了。可能是自己升级了软件版本、修改了全局指令文件，或者不小心污染了项目的上下文环境。为了洗脱自己的嫌疑，我们可以直接查看本地会话日志账单明细中的缓存命中
token 数，这个数值记录了本次请求直接复用了多少历史前缀。
服务端对缓存复用的校验非常严格，要求系统提示词、工具定义列表和项目规则文件必须完全一致，哪怕改动一个标点符号，前缀缓存就会失效重算。因此，这个数值天生就是检验本地环境是否变动的铅封。在
10 月下旬的审计中，作者检查了跨越异常时间窗口的 43
个新会话。日志显示，这些会话全都运行在同一个客户端版本上，而且每个新会话的首次请求命中的缓存
token 数，每一个都精确等于
29,503。这说明本地的系统提示词、工具定义和项目规范纹丝未动，变化百分之百来自云端。观察这个数字最大的用处，是让你立刻管住手，不要随意修改自己的全局提示词和项目规范文件。毕竟乱改本地配置不仅治不好云端的毛病，还会亲手打碎那九成以上的历史缓存复用，让你的订阅配额以十几倍的速度白白蒸发。
排除了本地配置变动之后，我们还可以用日志里的另一个元数据来探查云端隐藏的推理深度。模型在正式回答前会生成一段内部推演的思考块，服务端还会在思考块后面附上一个用于校验的加密签名。今年
3
月初，官方把默认接口里的思考块明文改成了隐藏状态，用户没法直接统计模型到底想了多少字，官方同时声称这一改动不影响模型的实际推理深度。
但是，加密签名仍然保存在本地日志中，且其字符长度与隐藏的思考文本的长度成正比。Stella
通过对比隐藏措施生效前的七千多个历史样本，发现了思考块附带的加密签名长度和实际思考字数之间存在
0.971
的高线性相关性。她用这个指标来测量这段时间的日志，发现模型的实际思考深度下降了
67%，并且在美西时间下午 5 点和晚上 7
点的用网高峰期出现了按小时规律性出现的降配谷底。在掌握了这个规律以后，平时遇到复杂的跨模块重构任务，就可以知道应该避开美西时间晚高峰，或者手动锁定最高的推理预算，避免在算力低谷期盲目死磕。
缓存命中数与加密签名长度分别从客户端配置和云端推理深度两个维度锁定服务端静默改动
没有标准答案的日常对话，怎么知道该不该继续重试？
确定了云端变更的时间节点只是第一步，还要量化它在日常开发中到底削弱了多少生产力。日常写代码没有标准答案，每天的开发任务也不一样，单看某次回答很难服人。我们用的技巧是不过问当前这一轮答得好不好，而是去统计下一轮人类真实的反馈。
在正常的协作流程里，如果模型干得漂亮，用户下一句就会接着布置新任务；如果模型理解错了或者改坏了代码，用户下一句就会出言纠正，或者模型在下一轮开头连忙道歉。10
月份的审计作者用脚本扫描了六千多条历史回答，专门提取这种相邻轮次的纠错信号。为了排除模型单纯客套道歉带来的噪音，作者还单独统计了用户亲自下场指出错误的刚性比例。
这些指标在 10 月 19
日前后出现了明显的断崖式变化：在这之前，需要用户出言纠正的回答仅占
3.3%；而在 10 月 19 日之后，这一比例直接飙升至
20.2%。即使只看每个新聊天会话的第一句话，不受长对话历史累积的影响，首轮出错率也翻了三倍多。
更让人头疼的是模型在收到纠错之后的恢复能力。在正常时期，只要用户点出问题所在，模型九成以上能在下一轮立刻改对，指出错误后紧接着下一句继续犯错的比例只有
10.0%。但在退化发生之后，这一连续再错率飙升到了 41.5%。
除了看纠错比例，人类自己敲进对话框的提问词频也是一面诚实的镜子。模型退化期间，我们会不自觉地减少对它的信任，从而改变自己的说话方式。Stella
查看了自己几万条本地记录中的提问用词，发现她让模型放心大胆地提交代码的
commit
和管理工单的指令减少了超过一半，而紧急喊停的
stop
接近翻倍，批评模型偷懒走捷径的
simplest
更是暴涨了 642%。虽然她在 2 月和 3
月亲手敲下的提问总数几乎一样，但因为模型反复报错重试，后台实际的接口请求总数膨胀了
80
倍，最终迫使她关停了手头的多智能体并发集群。这两个指标其实是在给日常开发亮红灯：一旦发现模型刚改完下一句还有四成概率继续错、自己开始频繁敲
stop
，就别在同一个会话窗口里继续跟模型讲道理重试了，那是在拿自己的配额和时间填无底洞，应当果断开新窗口或者换个切入思路。
思考变少了还是变多了？为什么看清病根才能避免用错药？
不少人一遇到这轮模型不在状态，就会下意识把推理强度拉满到
max
，幻想大力出奇迹。可如果你去对 4 月和 10
月的本地日志做审计会发现，同样是感觉模型变蠢，背后可能的病因恰恰相反，乱调杠杆只会更伤。
第一种是砍算力型退化，核心表现是不读文件直接乱改。当时云端调低了默认的推理预算，甚至在部分轮次直接把思考配额分成了零，模型为了省事不再查阅代码上下文。在
4 月的事故窗口里，模型每次修改代码前平均先读取文件的读写比，从正常时期的
6.6 次一路跌到了 2.0
次。连目标文件都没读过一眼就直接上手修改的比例，也从 6.2% 猛增到了
33.7%，经常把新代码直接插进注释块中间。对付这种缺算力导致的偷懒，手动调高推理档位，或者在本地挂个拦截脚本强迫它先读文件再动手修改，确实能立竿见影地解决问题。
另一种退化是上下文断路型，表现为算力不少、文件读了，但无视读到的内容。10
月的案例中，模型每次回答调用工具的中位数还是 6
次，高强度档位下计费的思考 token 中位数甚至从 1,060 涨到了
1,450，说明云端没有扣减推理算力，模型在工具调用上也没偷懒少干活，在读了文件之后直接无视了刚读到的内容。
为了证实这一点，作者从日志里抽出两百多条出错记录，抹去日期后打乱顺序做盲测分类。结果显示，模型凭空编造事实的比例几乎为零，唯独无视刚刚通过工具读进来的文件内容这一项，在退化窗口期暴涨了
8.2
倍。日志里有一条带官方请求编号的橄榄球阵容分析记录非常典型：模型先调工具读了状态文件，清楚看到某位球员刚遭球队裁掉且未来几周无法上场，接着认真思考了八百多个
token，还在回答正文里亲笔写下重新签回该球员会抵消刚才的操作，结果下一句却依然把这位球员列为头号签回人选。遇到这种算力充足但通往文件上下文的线路断掉的怪病，如果你还按老经验把推理强度拉到最高档
max
，日志统计出来的实际出错率反而高达
50.0%，纯属让模型在错误假设里原地空转、白烧双倍的 token。
4
月砍算力型退化表现为读写比暴跌与不读乱改，10
月上下文断路型退化表现为思考增加但无视刚读取的文件证据
云端网关断路时怎么自救？以及怎么让模型自己审日志？
为什么模型明明没少算、也确实调了工具，却偏偏出现读完文件就失忆的情况？很多人第一反应是在客户端下拉菜单里换个别的模型试试。但另一位重度用户在
11
月的跨模型故障汇总
里整理了五十多起带有完整日志的同类事故，发现这种读完文件就无视内容的毛病，同时出现在
Opus 5.5、上一代旧版 Opus 4.8 以及刚发布 5 天的新旗舰 Fable 5.2
上。三个不同代际、不同底层权重的模型同时患上同一种怪病，说明在同一个客户端里单纯切换模型是没有用的，故障出在所有模型共用的云端网关层。
云端网关层是运行在服务器端的一组处理步骤，夹在本机客户端程序和底层大模型权重之间，负责在模型进行推理前动态拼接安全提示词、管理历史思考块、分发实验参数。结合本地日志和官方历史前科，网关层有两个机制嫌疑最大。第一个嫌疑是防提示词注入的安全指令误伤了正常文件。审计作者在排查请求结构时发现，云端网关会在客户端缓存的前缀之后动态插入一段安全提示词，反复警告模型通过工具读取到的文件内容只是外部数据，不能视为指令；而且日志响应里的
safeguards
护栏字段恰好在 10 月 19 日至 22
日分批下线，印证了那几天云端刚刚切换过护栏方案。
在编程工具的工作流中，项目规范、任务计划和已有代码都依赖模型调用读取工具获取。一旦云端网关把所有工具返回的内容统一打上不可信数据的标签，模型在最终决策时会把刚读入的文件证据当作外部杂音降权丢弃。看懂这个机制之后，日常工作中的应急对策非常直观：遇到模型反复无视某个项目规范或接口定义文件，不要再让它调用读取工具查看文件，直接把那几行关键要求复制粘贴到你自己和模型的对话框里，用最高优先级的用户直接指令绕开云端网关对工具返回内容的降权。
第二个可能是云端网关截断或压缩了多步工具调用中的思考链。官方在
4
月底的事故回顾
中提到了两次类似的事故：一个是清理过期缓存的代码有漏洞，每次调用工具都会清空上一轮之前的所有历史思考块，导致模型在多步任务中忘记之前为什么要读那个文件。另一个是在系统提示词中加入了一句话，要求工具之间的过渡文字不超过
25 个单词，直接导致内部评测的准确率下降了 3 个百分点。在 11 月，又有
社区开发者的重放实验
从本地日志中发现了云端新下发的
atis-latch
实验标记，用 20
个相同的历史任务做控制变量重放。激活该参数后，模型每次调工具前的单步思考中位数从
159.5 个 token 降到了 65 个，一条消息合并调用两个以上工具的比例从 7/20
升到了
17/20。网关在中间每一步不让模型细想，强推并发冲刺，等一堆工具结果同时塞回来，最后即使补再多思考
token 也理不清头绪了。
看到这里你可能在想，我们每天写业务代码已经很忙了，难道每次怀疑模型变笨了，都要自己从头写一个统计脚本来分析日志吗？其实不用。在
Stella 4 月的审计报告末尾，Claude
留了一段附言：这份分析了六千多个会话、二十多万次工具调用的详尽报告，从头到尾都是
Stella 让 Claude 读取自己留在本地硬盘里的
.jsonl
日志自动算出来的。Claude
在附言里坦白说，它从内部视角感知不到自己的思考预算受限，只知道自己在写出更差的代码；直到它跑完自己的本地日志，才看清自己的读写比从
6.6 掉到了
2.0。模型在干活时对云端网关的改动毫无知觉，但它留在你硬盘里的会话日志却诚实地记下了一切。下次觉得编程助手不对劲，直接新开一个窗口，让它去扫一眼
~/.claude/projects/
下最近几天的日志，两分钟就能给自己开出一张明明白白的体检单。

items.text: innei published: 让 Agent 先问清楚、画出来、再证明：我的 Ryugi 工作流
items.title: 让 Agent 先问清楚、画出来、再证明：我的 Ryugi 工作流
items.content:
Ryugi (流儀)
—Ryugi is a set of interactive artifacts I built for coding agents. Whenever the agent needs to ask me questions or have me pick an approach, it puts them on interactive pages where I can answer directly: design decisions are written up as a document where I choose options item by item and leave sentence-level comments; UI proposals are laid out on a canvas for me to click and choose; and when the work is done, an acceptance page places approved designs side by side with live screenshots so I can approve or reject them group by group. Every choice I make on these pages feeds right back into the agent session that started it.
Repository
· Innei
536
ryugi
Ryugi (ryoo-ghee) — artifacts for coding agents: artboards of mockups, design docs, whiteboards, HTML benches and verify reports you comment on, with every comment sent back to the agent. Install artifacts only, or the full brainstorm → spec → TDD workflow. Claude Code, Codex and more.
JavaScript
The project here was the whiteboard inside my blog editor, haklex. Its editing features had always leaned on Excalidraw, which pulled in a heavy bundle and clashed with the rest of the editor's visual style. I wanted to drop the dependency and roll our own whiteboard around Excalidraw's data format, without touching a single field in existing articles.
From my opening sentence to `git push` took about half a day: two rounds of development, one release, and three downstream projects updated. I typed fewer than 20 messages in chat; wherever I had to make a call, it was turned into questions in a doc or mockups on a canvas. Here is how it went, step by step.
After one prompt: a doc that asks questions
My opening prompt was just one sentence: "Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures."
The agent first inspected the code to confirm the scope of changes, then opened a design doc and put its questions directly into it, without following up in the chat box.
The questions were embedded right inside the document, each with a recommended option and the reasoning behind it; all I had to do was click my choice on the page. The first question was a fork in the road that determined how big v1 should be—everything that followed depended on it. For two of the questions I skipped the recommendation, and the next round simply picked up from what I chose.
After each round, the conclusions were merged into a "Decided" section, noting whether I made the decision or the agent made it for me. I could tell at a glance which items needed another look.
Section 4 of the design doc, "Decided": each conclusion is tagged with who decided it
After two rounds, the document was fleshed out into a full design spec. Before handing it back to me, the agent had an uninvolved reviewer agent do a cold read; it resolved most of the feedback on its own, leaving just two questions for me to settle.
自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw · Ryugi
View “自研白板编辑器：替换 @excalidraw/excalidraw” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
"Should we discuss the UI?"
Once the document Q&A was done, I asked: "Should we discuss the UI?" The agent said yes—the design spec had marked the UI as "left to the implementer," but these are things you see every time you open the editor.
Text doesn't do UI justice, so it switched to a visual canvas: each group presented several options side by side, the recommended one highlighted with a red border, and sticky notes explaining the reasoning right beside them.
Round 1 decision fork on the UI canvas: three layout options side by side, with the recommended one outlined in red
Across two rounds and five groups, I went with the recommendations every time. With the options drawn out side by side, it was immediately clear which were good and which were bad. The selected mockups were linked into the design spec to guide both implementation and acceptance. Then I replied with "approve."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Once approved, I didn't look at code again
Once approved, the agent broke the design spec into 19 small tasks and tackled them one by one on a separate branch.
Each task followed the same rhythm: write a failing test, watch it fail, write the implementation to make it pass, and commit. Whenever the agent made a call on its own—like minor details that diverged slightly from the spec—it logged it in a ledger. When the chat grew too long and was summarized, it kept working right from that ledger.
For over an hour, I didn't type a single word.
Review, then the acceptance page
Once all 19 tasks were finished, the agent handed the branch over to an independent reviewer agent that had played no part in development. For every issue flagged, it reproduced it with a failing test before writing the fix.
Then it spun up the editor in a real browser, took screenshots and screen recordings, and put together an acceptance page: my approved canvas designs on the left, and how it actually looked running on the right.
Acceptance page: approved design, live screenshot, and screen recording side by side
All I had to do was review each group and approve or reject it. I left a comment on one mockup; it made the fix, took a new screenshot, and placed it right back in the same spot for me to review. Anything it couldn't verify was listed separately on the page, instead of being mixed in with "Completed."
白板编辑器界面 · Ryugi
View “白板编辑器界面” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Round two: starting from a reference image
Next, I wanted the whiteboard to look sharper. I pasted a reference image featuring clean headings, drop-shadowed sticky notes, and illustrative stickers, and asked whether stock Excalidraw could pull off that aesthetic.
It broke down the elements in the image one by one—what we could already draw, what capabilities were missing—and even guessed I might want an AI to do the drawing. I replied with one sentence: only build general-purpose drawing capabilities.
Next was the same process: open a new design doc, then three rounds of Q&A. In round three, putting rich-text cards on the whiteboard was my own idea. After a cold read, the reviewer agent flagged two questions that needed my call; the agent added its recommendations, I replied with two numbers, approved, and let it implement and review.
The acceptance page for this round measured directly against my reference image: the reference on the left, the recreation inside our editor on the right.
Round 2 acceptance: reference image side by side with the in-editor recreation
白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片 · Ryugi
View “白板绘制能力扩展：阴影、SVG 元素、富文本卡片” on Ryugi Cloud, a document artifact.
Ryugi
Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展 · Ryugi
View “Verify · 白板绘制能力扩展” on Ryugi Cloud, an artboard artifact.
Ryugi
Release, then downstream projects
With both rounds approved, I asked: "Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?" It cut a new release, then went through three projects using the editor one by one—bumping the dependency, running tests, and verifying in a browser that the whiteboard rendered properly.
Downstream results were posted right on the acceptance page as well, with one screenshot for light mode and one for dark.
The same whiteboard in downstream projects: light and dark mode
Throughout the entire process, logging in to authenticate the npm release was the only thing that needed my manual login—that was the one step the agent couldn't do for me.
What I actually said in the chat
Looking back, nearly everything I typed in chat over that half-day is captured right here:
Time
What I said
What happened next
12:26
Drop the excalidraw dependency and roll our own whiteboard based on its data structures
Read code, opened design doc
13:04
Should we discuss the UI?
Opened canvas for UI discussion
13:18
approve
Sliced tasks, started implementation
16:35
This looks about ready. Now let's work on extra features.
Compared against reference image, kicked off Round 2
16:38
Let's only build general-purpose drawing capabilities
Narrowed scope, opened new doc
17:04
approve
Implemented Round 2
17:56
Can we release now, and then adapt the downstream projects?
Published release, adapted downstream projects
20:06
push
Pushed to remote
Every other decision was made by clicking options in docs, picking mockups on a canvas, or signing off on the acceptance page. I didn't have to scroll through chat history to find what the agent said; every decision stayed on the page, and all the implementation and acceptance were checked against those same pages.
Boundaries
This workflow doesn't make judgment calls for me. If I skip an open-ended question, it fills in its best guess and flags it, leaving me to decide whether to review it. The acceptance page lists what it couldn't verify, and deciding whether to test further is up to me. What it does is put decisions right in front of me, so I can see at a glance what is settled and what isn't.
Ryugi is open source (
github.com/Innei/ryugi
). In your terminal, run
npx ryugi-artifacts install
, and select the agent you use to install it. The two design docs, canvas, and acceptance pages mentioned here are all public, so you can see them in their original form.

items.title: Optical payload delivery from Android to Linux - part 1. Manchester coding
items.content:
﷽
Hello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!
In my
previous DSP research
, we encoded bytes as sound. Welcome to a new series:
Optical payload delivery in Malware Development
. Over the next few parts, I will try to explore how to treat shellcode not as acoustic channel, but as an optical. This part sends a fixed
MEOW
frame from an Android screen as timed brightness changes. Since I have only my Thinkpad machines, a ThinkPad camera records the display; a C receiver checks the frame and dispatches
MEOW
to a linked Linux x86-64 assembly function that prints
Meow-meow!
.
As usual, let’s imagine that the Android app uses no permissions and makes no network connection. The receiver gets the video from the ThinkPad camera, FFmpeg extracts grayscale samples, and the C program validates the frame’s CRC before calling the fixed handler. The received bytes are a four-byte identifier; the receiver does not execute them as machine code yet.
The synthetic trace, generated MP4 and Moto G54 screenrecord decode
MEOW
and print
Meow-meow!
. I also completed the physical Android-screen-to-ThinkPad-camera run in Demo 2: the C receiver recovered
MEOW
, validated CRC
0x0ead
, and printed
Meow-meow!
.
the channel and concept
An endpoint can encode bytes as timed changes in screen brightness. A nearby camera records those changes, and a receiver reconstructs the frame.
Our physical path is:
Android app -> screen pixels -> light -> ThinkPad camera -> recorded video
|
v
C receiver + linked ASM <- grayscale samples <- FFmpeg
The Android screen sends the signal while the ThinkPad camera records it. FFmpeg converts the selected video region into one grayscale sample per frame, and the C receiver decodes that stream after capture.
frame and modulation
The frame is small:
AA AA AA AA | D3 91 | length: 1 byte | text: 1..32 bytes | CRC: 2 bytes
preamble
sync
high byte first
All bytes travel most significant bit first. The four-byte payload ID is
MEOW
. After CRC validation, the receiver dispatches that ID to one fixed handler. CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE uses polynomial
0x1021
, initial value
0xffff
, no reflection and no final XOR; it covers the length byte and payload.
We use Manchester encoding:
bit 0: gray 80 -> gray 176
bit 1: gray 176 -> gray 80
250 ms 250 ms
Every bit contains a transition. The receiver compares the mean intensity of the first half with the second half, so it does not need a single global dark/light threshold. It still needs enough contrast in the captured image.
One bit takes
0.5
seconds, giving a raw rate of
2 bits/s
. The
13
-byte
MEOW
frame takes
52
seconds, plus five seconds of leading gray and two seconds of trailing gray:
59
seconds total.
The full phone screen stays at gray
128
while idle and during the guards. During the frame it switches between gray
80
and
176
. The app requests a fixed screen brightness for the run and hides its prompt while transmitting, leaving the camera’s region of interest as a uniform patch.
mathematical model and decoding condition
First of all, we need some theoretical fundament. In the simple terms, the Android app changes the gray code across the screen. The phone display and ThinkPad camera transform it before the receiver sees a sample.
Let the transmitted gray code be \(u(t)\in\{80,128,176\}\). The display maps it to emitted luminance \(L(t)=F(u(t))\), where \(F\) models the panel’s static transfer curve, current brightness and color processing. For frame \(k\), the camera’s ROI value can be approximated as
\[\begin{aligned}
y_k = Q\!\Biggl(&a_k + g_k \frac{1}{T_e}\int_{t_k}^{t_k+T_e} L(\tau)\,d\tau \\
&{}+ n_k \Biggr).
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(T_e\) is exposure time, \(t_k\) is the exposure start, \(g_k\) is camera gain, \(a_k\) is offset, \(n_k\) represents sensor and image-processing noise, and \(Q\) includes quantization and video encoding. Rolling shutter makes \(t_k\) vary with image row; choosing a small ROI near the center of the phone screen limits, but does not eliminate, this effect. The grayscale bytes produced by FFmpeg are the \(y_k\) used by
receiver.c
.
Manchester mapping
Let a bit be \(b_i\in\{0,1\}\), a bit period be \(T_b=0.5\,\mathrm{s}\), and a half-bit period be \(T_h=T_b/2=0.25\,\mathrm{s}\). Define the light state \(m(t)\in\{0,1\}\), with gray levels \(G_L=80\) and \(G_H=176\). For time \(\tau\in[0,T_b)\) within the bit:
\[\begin{aligned}
m_i(\tau)&=\begin{cases}
b_i, & 0\leq\tau<T_h,\\
1-b_i, & T_h\leq\tau<T_b,
\end{cases} \\[0.4em]
u_i(\tau)&=G_L+(G_H-G_L)m_i(\tau).
\end{aligned}\]
Thus bit
0
is dark then light; bit
1
is light then dark. This is exactly the decision in
grayAt()
in
OpticalActivity.java
:
value
is \(b_i\), and the light state is \(b_i\) for the first half and \(1-b_i\) for the second.
Manchester coding is DC balanced over a complete bit. In the code domain:
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{T_b}\int_0^{T_b}m_i(\tau)\,d\tau&=\frac12, \\[0.4em]
\frac{1}{T_b}\int_0^{T_b}u_i(\tau)\,d\tau&=\frac{G_L+G_H}{2}=128.
\end{aligned}\]
The two bit values have the same average code value; the information is in the direction of the transition. Under a static display transfer function, both bit values also spend equal time at each emitted level, so their ideal average emitted luminance is \(\left(F(G_L)+F(G_H)\right)/2\), even if \(F\) is nonlinear. This can reduce sensitivity to a constant offset, but does not remove gain changes, exposure adaptation, clipping, display response or frame loss.
when the Manchester decision is correct
Assume the receiver has found the correct frame phase and half-bit duration, and its two central windows lie inside their corresponding transmitted halves. Let their noiseless measured means be \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\), with \(\Delta=\mu_H-\mu_L>0\). The differential statistic is
\[D_i=\bar y_{i,0}-\bar y_{i,1}.\]
Under the mapping above, \(D_i=+\Delta\) for bit
1
, and \(D_i=-\Delta\) for bit
0
. Therefore the sign of \(D_i\) recovers the bit exactly when the two means remain ordered. In the code,
means[0] > means[1]
returns
1
.
Now suppose the average error in each half-window is bounded by \(\eta\): \(\lvert \bar y_{i,j}-\mu_{i,j} \rvert\leq\eta\). For bit one, write the observed means as \(\bar y_{i,0}=\mu_H+\epsilon_0\) and \(\bar y_{i,1}=\mu_L+\epsilon_1\), where \(\lvert \epsilon_0 \rvert,\lvert \epsilon_1 \rvert\leq\eta\). Then
\[D_i=\Delta+\epsilon_0-\epsilon_1\geq\Delta-2\eta.\]
For bit zero, \(D_i\leq-\Delta+2\eta\). Thus \(\Delta>2\eta\) preserves the sign in either case. The implementation also rejects pairs whose differential magnitude is below 6 gray levels. A sufficient condition for both the correct sign and this threshold is
\[\Delta>6+2\eta.\]
This is a conditional correctness result for the Manchester decision. Honestly, it does not prove that a particular camera produces this contrast; \(\Delta\) and \(\eta\) must be measured from its actual recording. The implementation averages the central 60% of each half, matching the
0.2
and
0.8
bounds in
byte_at()

timing and exposure condition
The camera’s normalized sample stream is nominally \(f_s=30\) samples/s. Each half-bit therefore spans
\[N_h=f_sT_h=30\cdot0.25=7.5\text{ samples}.\]
The receiver searches \(\widehat N_h\) from
7.15
through
7.85
samples, stepping by
0.01
;
start
searches the phase in integer sample steps. If the true half duration is outside that range, or the capture contains a large timing discontinuity, this implementation can miss the frame.
For the central
60%
mean to avoid transitions, a sufficient timing condition for half \(j\) is
\[|e_j|+\frac{T_e}{2}+T_r+T_d < 0.2T_h,\]
where \(e_j\) is the sample-center timing error, \(T_e\) is exposure duration, \(T_r\) bounds display rise/fall smearing, and \(T_d\) is timing uncertainty from capture and frame-rate conversion. It includes up to half a normalized sample (about
16.7 ms
) from the receiver’s integer-sample phase search, plus any additional resampling or timestamp error. The right-hand side is
50 ms
here. This bound assumes a stable ROI, no clipping, and a bounded transition response; the current program does not read camera exposure or row timestamps and does not verify the inequality. It only searches a limited constant-rate timing range.
frame length, rate and error check
For payload length \(L\) bytes, the frame has \(N=L+9\) bytes: six preamble/sync bytes, one length byte, \(L\) data bytes and two CRC bytes. The frame has \(8N\) bits and \(16N\) half-bits. Since each half takes \(T_h\), the total duration including guards is
\[\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{total}}&=5\,\mathrm{s}+16(L+9)T_h+2\,\mathrm{s} \\
&=\bigl[7+4(L+9)\bigr]\,\mathrm{s}.
\end{aligned}\]
For
MEOW
, \(L=4\), so \(T_{\mathrm{total}}=59\,\mathrm{s}\). For
Meow-meow!
, \(L=10\), so \(T_{\mathrm{total}}=83\,\mathrm{s}\). The useful payload rate is
\[R_{\mathrm{useful}}=\frac{8L}{T_{\mathrm{total}}}\quad\text{bits/s},\]
or about
0.54 bits/s
for
MEOW
and
0.96 bits/s
for
Meow-meow!
. The raw Manchester bit rate is
2 bits/s
; framing and guards lower the useful rate.
CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE uses generator polynomial \(x^{16}+x^{12}+x^5+1\), initial remainder
0xffff
, and no reflection or final XOR. The implementation covers the length byte and payload. The receiver rejects a frame when the computed and received CRCs differ; CRC does not correct errors or authenticate the sender. The standard check value for ASCII
123456789
is
0x29b1
, a useful independent check of the CRC routine.
In polynomial terms, an error pattern \(E(x)\) goes undetected only if \(g(x)\) divides it. Since \(g\) has degree
16
, every nonzero burst error of length at most
16
bits is detected; longer error patterns can still be divisible by \(g\). This is error detection, not correction or authentication.

\[\Delta = \mu_{\mathrm{light}} - \mu_{\mathrm{dark}}.\]

For repeated transmissions, I count \(x\) frames whose CRC passes and whose recovered text matches the sent text, out of \(n\) attempts. The observed packet success fraction is
\[\hat p = \frac{x}{n}.\]
To show the uncertainty in that fraction, I use the 95% Wilson interval. With \(z=1.96\), its center \(c\) and half-width \(h\) are
\[\begin{aligned}
c&=\frac{\hat p+z^2/(2n)}{1+z^2/n}, \\[0.4em]
h&=\frac{z}{1+z^2/n}

Bit-error rate needs individual bit decisions:
\[\widehat{\mathrm{BER}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{wrong}}}{N_{\mathrm{sent}}}.\]
